(Libby Kamrowski Kenny/Staff Photographer) LEWISTON — It wasn’t the result that Shawna Haley-Bear and Caleb Bear had hoped for. The mother and son pair from Poland won tickets to the 6 a.m. balloon launch Friday morning that kicked off the 32nd Lewiston-Auburn Balloon Festival , but high winds canceled all balloon flights Friday morning. Haley-Bear entered a contest for the tickets through Dirigo Credit Union, the festival’s special shape balloon sponsor. The contest asked entrants a question: If you could create any shape balloon, what would it be? Haley-Bear chose the “Hopeful” sign. “There’s so much that’s good in Lewiston-Auburn that we don’t think about, so I feel like that sign makes me think about the good stuff. The stuff that unites us and makes us a community,” said Haley-Bear on Friday morning, who said she has attended the festival for years. While morning festivalgoers and pilots were disappointed by the grounding, the much larger gathering in the park for the evening launch Friday was treated to a successful launch that saw several balloons soar into the air. Advertisement Friday morning, the festival’s balloonmeister made the final call shortly before 6 a.m. on whether balloons could go up; the winds were deemed too fierce to fly. Despite that, several balloon pilots inflated their balloons and stayed tethered to the ground as hundreds of early-morning festivalgoers watched at Simard-Payne Memorial Park. To test the winds at various elevations, a small balloon is released 500 feet in the air. By using technology connected to the balloon, the wind speed is measured. Wind speed Friday morning measured 20 mph. The ideal winds are around 5 to 8 mph, said Bruce Byberg, the balloonmeister. The view from inside the balloon: America One pilot Barry DiLibero inflates the balloon Friday morning during the Lewiston-Auburn Balloon Festival in Simard-Payne Memorial Park in Lewiston. DiLibero also owns Flighthouse, the lighthouse balloon being shown at the festival, and is based out of Pennsylvania. (Libby Kamrowski Kenny/Staff Photographer) View 16 photos “When the sun comes up and heats the earth, the lower winds mix with the higher winds, so that 20 miles per hour will come closer to the surface. We don’t want to land at 10-20 miles per hour,” said Byberg. Beth and Joe Hamilton were there Friday morning, having traveled from Florida to fly their balloon “Last One.” The couple of 55 years started piloting after Joe bought Beth a ride for her birthday. Advertisement Beth received her pilot’s license in California and Joe trained in Albuquerque. Both climates are more predictable for flying, in comparison to Maine, they said, but they’ve attended the Lewiston-Auburn festival since the very beginning. When asked, after all their years ballooning, whether they get upset when weather prevents them from flying, they were emphatic. “Hell yeah,” said Beth. “But that’s the life of the balloonist. The weather. You learn early, you have to be patient.” Festival organizers were hopeful the weather would clear for the night and weekend flights. Come 4 p.m., the weather fulfilled those hopes and it didn’t take long for the festival grounds to fill up. Just 10 minutes after the carnival adjacent to the festival grounds opened, there were lines for the big rides. Kids screamed from the stomach-churning Genesis ride and from the Pharaoh’s Journey just around the corner. Mary Ellen Pinkham was there with her husband and three grandchildren: 13, 9 and 6 years old. The family had come from Norridgewock to their first-ever balloon festival. Advertisement “We’ve been wanting to go to the big balloon festival down in Albuquerque,” Pinkham said, the kids off on various rides, “so we figured we’d come to this one and see how we like it.” The verdict? They loved it. Loved the carnival, the food and the prospect of seeing the big balloons rising into the night. Pinkham loves the sight of the balloons from the grounds, but was she hustling to get a ride in one? “Not me,” she said, laughing at her own fears. “My best friend went on a balloon ride and said it was great until it was time to land, at which point it was just a controlled crash.” And speaking of hard landings, Pinkham was also there to see the skydivers, who were expected to jump from a plane at 5 p.m. and land on the festival grounds five minutes later. At 5 p.m. exactly, three dots appeared next to a plane that had been circling above. For several minutes, those dots grew larger, and each was accompanied by a flag that flapped and rippled all the way down. Advertisement The skydivers landed one-buy-one at about 5:05 p.m., each drawing cheers. The band playing at that moment on the festival stage, JoAnna Hughes and the Ditch Lilies, even paused their show to give the divers a round of applause. All around the festival grounds, waiting for the arrival of the balloons, hundreds of visitors were busy with one activity or another. Lines at Damn Yankee Balloons were long as kids waited their turns to enter a half-inflated balloon transformed into a bouncy house. A dozen or so danced in front of the stage as JoAnna Hughes and her crew pounded out country and rock. Dave and Lisa, a couple from New Gloucester, were digging it all from their lawn chairs set up near the far end of Simard-Payne Memorial Park. There was one thing specifically that brought them here. Advertisement “I love the balloons,” said Dave. “It seems like a safe atmosphere and the people are friendly.” Lisa, meanwhile, tended to agree with Mary Ellen Pinkham on the matter of hot air balloons. “I like looking at them,” she said. “But I like to keep my feet on something steady.” As it closed in on dark, the chatter across the festival grounds seemed almost singular minded: Would the balloons be able to launch this evening? Or was the stiff breeze blowing across the grounds still too great a risk. Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline was of a like mind. All in all, the festival’s opening day was a big success. But what it needed most was calm and cooperative weather. “So many smiles and beautiful weather,” the mayor said, “except for the damn wind.” Advertisement Maybe the mayor’s ire helped out a little. Just before 6 p.m., it was announced that balloons would, in fact, launch. A ripple of excitement went through the crowd, but then the wind picked back up again and the chance of a launch seemed uncertain again. Some pilots decided to take to the skies. Such is the fickle nature of hot air balloons. Some might say it’s part of their charm. For more information on the festival and schedule, visit laballoonfest.org/festival/schedule . That realization sends thousands of learners away from the language every year. But here's what those learners never discovered: the cases aren't the obstacle. The approach to teaching them is. The Case Problem Is a Teaching Problem, Not a Language Problem Polish's grammatical case system is frequently cited as one of the most daunting features for English speakers. And statistically, that reputation is earned — the Foreign Service Institute classifies Polish as a Category III language, requiring roughly 1,100 hours to reach professional working proficiency. But that number is an average, and averages obscure a lot. Learners who approach Polish cases as isolated grammar rules consistently struggle longer than those who encounter them through high-frequency sentence patterns. A practical illustration: instead of memorizing that the genitive case is used after negation, a learner repeatedly exposed to sentences like "Nie mam czasu" (I don't have time) and "Nie widzę problemu" (I don't see a problem) internalizes the pattern naturally. The rule becomes a description of something already known, not a prescription to memorize. This is exactly the methodological difference that separates learners who plateau at A2 from those who push through to B2 and beyond. Structured polish classes with experienced instructors are designed around this distinction — building grammatical intuition through context rather than forcing abstract rule memorization from the outset. What Adult Learners Get Wrong About Their Own Progress One of the most common misconceptions among adult Polish learners is measuring progress by what they understand rather than what they can produce . Passive comprehension grows quickly in the first months. Active production — speaking and writing with accuracy — lags significantly behind. Learners mistake the first for the second and grow frustrated when conversation doesn't come naturally after weeks of study. The solution isn't studying harder. It's restructuring the ratio of input to output. Professionals who successfully reached B2 or C1 in Polish typically shifted to a 60/40 ratio of active production exercises to passive input by the time they hit the intermediate stage. That means more speaking practice, more written assignments with corrections, and more structured feedback from qualified teachers. Reading Polish Proficiency Levels as a Career Map Language certification levels aren't just academic milestones — they map directly onto professional and legal realities in 2026. Understanding what each level actually unlocks helps learners invest their time where it counts most. At B1 , a learner can handle most everyday communication and is typically eligible to apply for Polish permanent residency after meeting other criteria. At B2 , professional conversations in most office environments become manageable, and opportunities in Polish-speaking workplaces open substantially. The C1 level is where the real shift happens for career-oriented learners. C1 proficiency in Polish signals near-native command of the language — the ability to understand implicit meaning, navigate complex professional texts, and produce nuanced written and spoken content without significant errors. For roles in law, academia, senior management in Polish companies, or specialized fields requiring precise communication, C1 is often the de facto standard. Preparing for and passing a c1 exam demonstrates a level of commitment and competence that carries genuine weight with Polish employers and institutions. The Preparation Gap That Most Learners Discover Too Late One pattern emerges repeatedly among learners who attempt C1 without structured guidance: they underestimate the writing component. While speaking and reading skills can develop organically through immersion and practice, the formal writing required at C1 — analytical essays, formal correspondence, structured arguments — demands deliberate, corrected practice over months, not weeks. Learners who begin focused C1 preparation at least six months before their target exam date consistently outperform those who attempt to compress preparation into two or three months. The difference isn't raw ability — it's the time required for corrective feedback to reshape writing habits. Three Profiles That Illustrate What Structured Learning Actually Delivers Abstract advice lands differently when grounded in recognizable situations. Here are three composite profiles based on common learner trajectories: The Relocating Professional: A Ukrainian IT specialist relocating to Warsaw in 2026 joined a structured B1 course after six months of app-based self-study. The self-study had built solid vocabulary but left grammar fragmented. Within four months of structured classes, the gaps were addressed systematically and the B1 exam was passed on the first attempt. The Academic Applicant: A researcher from Germany needed C1 Polish to qualify for a position at a Kraków university. Working with a program that combined intensive grammar review with academic writing practice, she reached exam-ready level in eight months — faster than she had anticipated. The Heritage Learner: A second-generation Polish speaker from the United States had conversational fluency but no formal grammar foundation. Targeted coursework helped him convert passive knowledge into certified proficiency, reaching B2 in approximately five months of structured study. Each of these paths is different, but the common thread is the same: structured, corrected, professionally guided learning compressed the timeline significantly compared to self-directed alternatives. Choosing the Right Entry Point Without Wasting the First Month The single most time-saving decision a new Polish learner can make is an honest placement assessment before beginning any structured program. Starting at the wrong level — either too low or too high — costs weeks of misaligned effort. A course that's too easy builds false confidence; one that's too advanced creates discouragement before real progress begins. Quality language institutes conduct diagnostic assessments that evaluate reading comprehension, grammatical accuracy, and spoken production separately, because these skills rarely develop at equal rates. The result is a placement that challenges learners appropriately while building on existing strengths — which is, ultimately, how sustainable progress is made in one of Europe's most demanding languages. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, Putin sounded uncompromising and confident at his talks with the US envoys By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,Â Reporting from Moscow Published 13 November 2026 Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine. That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire. And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace? The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace." Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia. What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War. The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 â the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin. What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia". That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them. But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow. "In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week. "Our proposals were almost laughed at. "Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement." The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire". "The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture." Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table. Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia. This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US. After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks. But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken. "Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident. You can see why. The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him. And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe. And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield. The Russian economy is under increasing pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages. But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.
